prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGALORE, India (CNN) -- Two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma, an Indian toddler born with four arms and four legs, made her first public appearance Tuesday, a week after surgeons in India successfully removed her additional limbs. Doctors said Lakshmi was recovering well as she appeared Tuesday at a news conference. Lakshmi, wearing a plaster cast on her legs to keep her feet up and her legs together to help her wounds heal, was carried into a news conference Tuesday as her doctors announced she was being released from intensive care. "She is coping very well," lead surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil said. "She is being carried around by her mother and her father." Several of her doctors, all of them smiling, described her recovery over the past week "very steady and good progress," one saying she is "out of the woods" as far as serious medical issues are concerned.  Watch the recovering little girl meet the media » . The operation a week ago lasted 27 hours and involved a team of some 30 surgeons, all specialists in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics, and plastic surgery, working in eight-hour shifts. Lakshmi's extra limbs were part of a conjoined twin which stopped developing in the womb. It had a torso and limbs but no head, and was joined to Lakshmi at the pelvis. Doctors said that without the surgery, Lakshmi would have been unlikely to survive beyond early adolescence. The surgery involved the removal of the extra limbs and the repositioning of Lakshmi's organs. When Lakshmi was born into her poor, rural Indian family, villagers in the remote settlement of Rampur Kodar Katti in the northern state of Bihar believed she was sacred. As news of her birth spread, locals queued for a blessing from the baby. Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named the girl after the Hindu goddess of wealth who has four arms. However, they were forced to keep her in hiding after they were approached by men offering money in exchange for putting their daughter in a circus. The couple, who earn just $1 a day as casual laborers, wanted her to have the operation but were unable to pay for the rare procedure, which had never before been performed in India. After Patil visited the girl in her village from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore, the hospital's foundation agreed to fund the $200,000 operation. Planning for the surgery took a month, Patil said, and Lakshmi spent that month in the hospital. Many villagers, however, remained opposed to surgery and were planning to erect a temple to Lakshmi, whom they still revere as sacred. E-mail to a friend .

BANGALORE, India (CNN) — One week after undergoing successful surgery in India to remove four extra limbs, two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma appeared before the public for the first time on Tuesday.

At a news conference, physicians said the Indian child—who was born with four arms and four legs—was healing well and had been moved out of intensive care. She was carried into the room wearing a plaster cast designed to hold her legs together and keep her feet elevated while her wounds healed.

Lead surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil said Lakshmi was handling her recovery “very well” and could now be carried by both her mother and father. Her smiling medical team described her improvement during the previous week as steady and positive. One doctor said she was “out of the woods” regarding major medical complications.

The procedure, performed a week earlier, took 27 hours. Approximately 30 surgeons specializing in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics and plastic surgery worked in eight-hour rotations.

Lakshmi’s additional arms and legs belonged to a conjoined twin that had ceased developing before birth. The undeveloped twin, attached to her pelvis, had a torso and limbs but no head. Surgeons removed the extra limbs and rearranged Lakshmi’s organs. Doctors said that without the operation, she probably would not have lived beyond her early teenage years.

Lakshmi was born to an impoverished family in Rampur Kodar Katti, a remote rural community in Bihar, northern India. Villagers regarded her as holy, and after word of her birth circulated, local residents lined up to receive the infant’s blessing.

Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named her after Lakshmi, the four-armed Hindu goddess associated with wealth. Later, the family had to conceal the child when men offered them money to display her in a circus.

Although her parents wanted the surgery, they could not afford the unusual operation, which had never previously been carried out in India. The couple earned only $1 per day doing casual labor.

Patil traveled from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore to visit Lakshmi in her village. Afterward, the hospital’s foundation agreed to cover the procedure’s $200,000 cost. According to Patil, preparations took one month, during which Lakshmi remained hospitalized.

Despite the operation, many people in her village continued to view her as sacred. Some opposed the surgery and were making plans to build a temple dedicated to her.

A video showed the recovering child meeting the media, and the original report also included an option to e-mail the story to a friend.

The surgery lasted approximately 27 hours and involved a multidisciplinary team of around 30 medical specialists. Lakshmi Tatma was born in 2005 to a poor laboring family in rural Bihar, India. She had an extremely rare form of conjoined twinning called **ischiopagus parasitic twinning**: an incompletely developed, headless twin was joined to her at the pelvis, leaving her with four arms and four legs and causing serious problems involving her pelvis, spine, kidneys, and other organs.

In 2007, when she was two, a large surgical team at Sparsh Hospital in Bangalore carried out a complex operation lasting roughly 27 hours. Doctors separated the parasitic twin, removed the extra limbs, and reconstructed parts of Lakshmi’s pelvis and internal anatomy. She survived and recovered well, although she later needed rehabilitation and additional treatment for orthopedic problems. She eventually learned to stand and walk with assistance and was able to attend school.

Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, had few financial resources and initially struggled to obtain specialized care. In their village, however, Lakshmi’s unusual appearance inspired religious reverence. Because the Hindu goddess **Lakshmi** is commonly depicted with four arms, some villagers believed the child was the goddess’s incarnation or a divine sign. People visited, prayed to her, and offered gifts, which helped explain both her name and why she was regarded as sacred.

**BREAKING NEWS | November 14, 2007**

# Lakshmi Tatma recovering well one week after marathon surgery

**BANGALORE, India** — Two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma is making a better-than-expected recovery one week after surgeons at Narayana Health City removed a partially developed parasitic twin from her body during a marathon 27-hour operation.

Lead surgeon **Dr. Sharan Patil** said Lakshmi was stable, breathing without a ventilator and beginning to take food.

> “Her progress has been beyond our expectations,” Patil told reporters. “She is very stable.”

Doctors said the child was moving her remaining arms and legs and showing no immediate signs of a serious post-operative infection. She remained under close observation, however, because of the scale and complexity of the reconstruction.

## More than 30 specialists involved

The operation began on November 6 and ended the following day. A multidisciplinary team of more than 30 doctors and other medical personnel participated at the Sparsh Hospital facility within Narayana Health City, outside Bangalore.

Lakshmi was born joined at the pelvis to an incompletely formed, headless twin. The rare condition left her appearing to have four arms and four legs. The parasitic twin shared parts of Lakshmi’s blood supply and was attached to her spine and pelvic region.

During the operation, surgeons separated the twin, divided shared tissues and blood vessels, reconstructed Lakshmi’s pelvis and repositioned organs. Orthopaedic, neurosurgical, plastic-surgery and paediatric teams worked in stages to reduce blood loss and protect her nerves and remaining limbs.

> “Lakshmi is responding very well to the treatment,” Patil said, while cautioning that she would still require prolonged rehabilitation and further corrective procedures.

Doctors expect future treatment to include physiotherapy and possible operations involving her hips, pelvis and feet. Patil has said the immediate objective was not simply to remove the parasitic twin, but to give Lakshmi the best possible chance of eventually standing and walking.

## Charitable foundation covered the cost

Lakshmi’s parents, labourers from a poor rural family in Bihar, could not afford the highly specialised treatment. The operation and hospital care—reported to be worth several million rupees—were provided without charge to the family.

Funding came through the hospital’s charitable arm, the **Sparsh Foundation**, with the medical institution and participating specialists absorbing or underwriting the cost. The foundation was established to make complex reconstructive and orthopaedic treatment available to children whose families lack the means to pay.

Hospital officials said Lakshmi would continue to receive post-operative care and rehabilitation through the same charitable arrangement.

Lakshmi was named after the four-armed Hindu goddess of wealth, and some people in her home village had regarded her unusual appearance as divine. Her parents nevertheless sought surgery after doctors warned that the additional limbs and shared anatomy would place increasing strain on her body and could ultimately threaten her life.

For now, Patil said, the medical team was encouraged—but remained watchful.

> “We are very happy with her recovery,” he said. “There is still a long way to go.”
